intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. The notes under each slide explain it, give you something to remember and warn you where people slip. Work the exercises in pencil, test yourself with the questions, and write your own notes in the margins.

sections.title: Why participation
sections.big_idea: Participation is a question of **who decides at each stage**, and the method's name tells you less than the answer.
in_plain_words: Participatory methods put the people a study or programme concerns in charge of parts of the inquiry: defining questions, producing information, interpreting it and deciding what follows. In extractive work the data leaves the village. In participatory work the analysis happens where the data was produced.

People defend this on three different grounds, instrumental, rights-based and epistemic, and each implies its own test of success. In India the Gram Sabha has legal powers, so participation is also a legal matter. Organic participation grows from activists; **induced participation** is engineered by projects, and Mansuri and Rao found it builds little lasting cohesion.

children.label: Instrumental
items: Fails if results are no better

children.label: Rights-based
items: Fails if meetings cannot change anything

children.label: Epistemic
items: Fails if it repeats the survey

key_terms.meaning: Outsiders set questions and take the data away.
How much control people hold in research.
Body of all registered voters in a panchayat area.
Efforts by civic activists, such as MKSS hearings.
Participation engineered by projects or schemes.

worked_example.title: Which justification is this?
worked_example.setup: Three project proposals each defend participation differently.
steps: Proposal A says local knowledge will make the project cheaper and better targeted. That is the instrumental case, so it must show results.
Proposal B says villagers have a right to a say, citing Part IX and PESA. That is the rights-based case, so it must show power moved.
Proposal C says residents know things surveys miss. That is the epistemic case, so it must show accuracy gains.
For each, write down what evidence would count as failure.
worked_example.answer: Instrumental, rights-based and epistemic respectively, each with its own test.

mistakes: Calling an exercise participatory because it uses a PRA tool. Every method can be run extractively.
Defending a project on all three grounds and measuring none of them.
Treating a survey as always inferior. Fixed questions are needed for comparability, and a mixed design can use both.
Ignoring the state's Panchayat Raj Act when working with a gram panchayat.

recall.q: What question decides whether inquiry is participatory?
recall.a: Who decides at each stage.

recall.q: Name the three justifications for participation.
recall.a: Instrumental, rights-based and epistemic.

recall.q: What is the difference between organic and induced participation?
recall.a: Organic grows from civic activists; induced is engineered through projects or schemes.

recall.q: What did Mansuri and Rao find about induced participation?
recall.a: Little evidence that it builds long-lasting cohesion.

recall.q: Which Article gives the Gram Sabha its powers, and where do those powers come from?
recall.a: Article 243A, which leaves them to state law.

sections.title: Origins: Freire, Fals-Borda, Chambers
sections.big_idea: Participatory methods grew from **Freire's dialogue, action research and Chambers's field practice**, and success then watered them down.
in_plain_words: Freire criticised banking education and proposed problem-posing dialogue that leads to critical consciousness. Fals-Borda carried this into participatory action research, where ordinary people produce valid knowledge and the community owns the results. Rahman supplied a South Asian strand through the Bhoomi Sena study.

Chambers argued that outsiders misread rural poverty and moved from rapid appraisal to participatory appraisal. India was a place where PRA was invented and tested, around 1990. Within a decade it became a donor requirement, compressed into days, which invited Cooke and Kothari's critique. **Methods dropped Freire's political aim** more often than his tools.

diagram.caption: five sources of the participatory tradition

key_terms.meaning: Teacher deposits knowledge into passive pupils.
Critical consciousness, then action on oppression.
Participatory action research owned by the community.
Rapid rural appraisal: quicker learning by outsiders.
Participatory appraisal: local people's own analysis.

worked_example.title: RRA or PRA?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: two field teams each call their work 'PRA'.
steps: Team 1 draws charts, analyses them back at the office and writes a report for the agency. The aim is quicker learning by outsiders: RRA.
Team 2 convenes village groups who analyse their own situation and keep the maps. Outputs are held locally, plus a report. This is PRA.
The slide warns the line blurs, so ask who analyses.
worked_example.answer: Team 1 is RRA with chart paper; Team 2 is PRA.

mistakes: Treating the RRA and PRA contrast as exact. The deck calls it a teaching simplification.
Keeping Freire's tools while dropping his political aim, as when a wealth ranking only targets a subsidy.
Running a consultation where the officer talks for forty minutes and then asks for questions, and calling it dialogue.
Compressing slow, open-ended methods into a few days to meet project timelines.

recall.q: What is banking education?
recall.a: The teacher deposits knowledge into pupils treated as empty accounts.

recall.q: What does PAR ask of researchers?
recall.a: To return findings in usable forms and accept being judged by the people they worked with.

recall.q: What was Chambers's central theme in Putting the Last First?
recall.a: Rural poverty is often unseen or misperceived by outsiders who are not themselves rural and poor.

recall.q: Where was the 1991 workshop reported in RRA Notes 13 held?
recall.a: Bangalore.

recall.q: What did Cooke and Kothari's 2001 volume do?
recall.a: Turned the critique of domination against participatory practice itself.

sections.title: Ladders and typologies
sections.big_idea: Typologies show **which degree of participation** happened, and they describe who holds power without saying which level is right.
in_plain_words: 'The community participated' can mean residents were told about a road after sanction, or that they chose it and checked the bills. Arnstein's eight-rung ladder groups the answers into nonparticipation, tokenism and citizen power. Pretty's seven types run from passive to self-mobilisation, and White asks who wants participation and why.

The three differ in audience and question. Arnstein asks how much power citizens hold; Pretty asks whether people's learning and action change; White maps competing interests, so one committee can be nominal, instrumental and representative at once. A typology cannot tell you which level is right, and **its labels should point to a fix**.

key_terms.meaning: People are heard but the powerful keep the decision.
Groups formed to meet a project's set objectives.
Joint analysis leading to action and local control.
White's form serving legitimation and display.
White's form serving sustainability and voice.

worked_example.title: Label the Pipalgaon plan
worked_example.setup: The employment scheme's village plan was approved in a gram sabha that the Dalit hamlet did not attend (illustrative case from the deck).
steps: Arnstein: people were told after the event, so rung 3, informing, in the tokenism band.
Pretty: people are told what has happened, so passive participation.
White: the block office wanted legitimation, so nominal.
The three labels agree on the remedy: hold a ward-level meeting in the hamlet first.
worked_example.answer: Informing, passive and nominal, all pointing to a meeting in the hamlet first.

mistakes: Using a typology to prove a level is correct. Some decisions may properly rest with engineers.
Treating 'citizens' as one group, the blind spot Arnstein's ladder leaves.
Mistaking a functional committee for an interactive one because both keep minutes.
Using White's table as a quick rating scale. It is harder to use that way.

recall.q: Name Arnstein's three bands.
recall.a: Nonparticipation, tokenism and citizen power.

recall.q: What separates functional from interactive participation in Pretty's scheme?
recall.a: Where the objectives came from and whether the group would act without the project.

recall.q: What question does White ask that the ladders skip?
recall.a: What interest each side has in a given form of participation.

recall.q: How can you test whether a committee is interactive?
recall.a: Ask for minutes from meetings the project did not attend.

recall.q: What should you write down before a participatory exercise?
recall.a: Who wants it and why, for each actor.

sections.title: PRA tools I: maps, walks, timelines
sections.big_idea: Visual, group-based tools let people analyse their own world, but **the map shows whoever drew it**.
in_plain_words: PRA tools rely on drawing on the ground with sticks, seeds and powder, so literacy is no condition for taking part. The social map shows who lives where, the resource map shows access to land, water and forest, the transect walk checks the ground with its users, mobility maps show who can reach what, and timelines record the village's own history.

Each tool has a typical failure. Men from the main village pick up the stick first and draw the Dalit hamlet as a smudge. A resource map can later be read as evidence of encroachment. **Output without a record of who drew it** is weak evidence, so note date, participants, who held the marker and what was disputed.

diagram.caption: building a social map in six steps

key_terms.meaning: Map of households, hamlets and landmarks drawn by residents.
Map of land, water and forest and who uses them.
Planned walk crossing every zone with residents.
Approaching one question with several tools and groups.
Map of where people travel and who cannot.

worked_example.title: How much did the second map add?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative figures from the deck: the first Pipalgaon map showed 610 households, and mapping in the hamlet across the stream added 140.
steps: Combine the two maps: 610 + 140 = 750 households.
Express the addition against the first map: 140 ÷ 610 = 0.23.
The hamlet map also found two handpumps the main village believed were working.
Treat the gap as a finding and keep both maps.
worked_example.answer: 750 households in all; the hamlet map added about 23% to the first count.

mistakes: Running one mapping group and letting the first people to pick up the stick set the picture.
Leaving the original at the site without agreeing in advance who keeps a resource map and what it may be used for.
Photographing a map with no note of who drew it or how many took part.
Treating a timeline's dates as exact. Record the anchor event and present it as the village's account.

recall.q: Why do PRA tools use drawing on the ground?
recall.a: They rely on visual and oral communication so that literacy is not needed to take part.

recall.q: Why cross-check a social map against the voter list?
recall.a: A village-drawn map often lists households that official lists miss, so comparing the two reveals gaps.

recall.q: What should you do if the first map smudges a hamlet?
recall.a: Run separate groups by hamlet and gender, then walk to the hamlet and compare maps.

recall.q: What does a mobility map reveal?
recall.a: Constraints that a list of services hides, such as seasonal migration.

recall.q: Name three things to record about a PRA session.
recall.a: Any three of: date, place, tool, participants by group, who held the marker, disagreements, participants' reading.

sections.title: PRA tools II: calendars, ranking, Venn
sections.big_idea: Calendars, clocks, rankings and diagrams show **when, who and what matters**, each with a caution about exposure.
in_plain_words: A seasonal calendar plots rainfall, labour, illness, cash and migration by month, and an activity clock shows whose time is scarce. Both tell you when people can attend meetings. Wealth ranking sorts household cards into locally defined piles, a chapati diagram shows institutions by size and distance, and matrix ranking scores options against criteria the group chooses.

Ranking neighbours in public can shame them, and labels travel. Use small separate panels, number the cards and say what the ranking will decide. Sequence tools so each output feeds the next, and run each separately by gender and hamlet. A change in order between groups is **the disagreement the gram sabha needs to discuss**.

spokes.label: Seasonal calendar
spokes.sub: when people are busy or sick

key_terms.meaning: Variables plotted by month using seeds or stones.
A typical day described hour by hour.
Households sorted into locally defined piles.
Venn diagram of institutions by size and distance.
Options scored against criteria the group chooses.

worked_example.title: Check the matrix totals
worked_example.setup: Illustrative scores from the deck, 0 to 5, for four priority works against cost, benefit to the poorest, water saved and speed.
steps: Farm ponds: 3 + 1 + 4 + 4 = 12.
Desilting the common tank: 4 + 4 + 4 + 2 = 14.
Fodder plots: 3 + 4 + 1 + 3 = 11.
Concrete lane: 2 + 1 + 0 + 5 = 8.
Rank them: the tank is first for this group. Rerun the matrix with other groups.
worked_example.answer: Tank 14, ponds 12, fodder plots 11, lane 8; rerun with the Dalit hamlet and women's group.

mistakes: Calling a gram sabha at harvest or the main migration season. Those who stayed are rarely the poorest.
Naming households on the cards or on anything that leaves the room.
Using ranking to replace legal criteria for ration cards or pensions. It can only help identify households to help apply.
Scoring options with one group and treating the result as the village's priority.

recall.q: What does a seasonal calendar show?
recall.a: Hungry months, cash shortages, sickness peaks and when people cannot attend meetings.

recall.q: What do circle size and distance mean in a chapati diagram?
recall.a: Size shows importance and distance from the centre shows accessibility.

recall.q: Name two safeguards for wealth ranking.
recall.a: Any two of: small panels apart from the main meeting, numbered cards, several panels averaged, telling panels what the ranking decides.

recall.q: Why compare local piles with the below-poverty-line list?
recall.a: Households poor by local criteria and absent from the official list are a common useful finding.

recall.q: How should tools be sequenced?
recall.a: So each output feeds the next, such as map, then wealth ranking, then matrix ranking.

sections.title: Participatory governance in India
sections.big_idea: Indian law gives the Gram Sabha **defined powers that vary by state**, and real cases show both the reach and the limits of participation.
in_plain_words: The 73rd Amendment made the Gram Sabha constitutional, but Article 243A leaves its powers to state law. PESA gives each Gram Sabha in Scheduled Areas specific powers over plans, beneficiaries, fund certification and consultation on land. The 2025 employment Act repeals MGNREGA from 1 July 2026 and keeps assemblies in planning and audit.

Cases test the law. In Niyamgiri twelve Gram Sabhas rejected a mining project and the ministry refused clearance. Kerala opened a whole state's plan to village assemblies, and its official evaluation found participation that was real and partly captured. Pune's ward budget is simple and durable but thin on deliberation. **Money that follows the vote** separates budgeting from consultation.

children.label: Constitution
items: Art 243A: Gram Sabha powers via state law

children.label: VB-G RAM G Act 2025
items: Records open to the Gram Sabha

diagram.caption: three instruments, three sets of powers

key_terms.meaning: Inserted Part IX and the Eleventh Schedule, in force 24 April 1993.
Extends Part IX to Scheduled Areas with modifications.
Residents vote on a defined share of a budget.
Kerala's state-level decentralised planning from 1996.
Odisha case where Gram Sabhas rejected mining in 2013.

worked_example.title: Reading the Kerala evaluation
worked_example.setup: The Programme Evaluation Organisation reported that non-attending beneficiaries were more common above the poverty line (34.7%) than below it (25.1%). The same report found 29% overall.
steps: Find the gap between the two groups: 34.7 − 25.1 = 9.6 percentage points.
The above-poverty-line group is more likely to receive benefits without attending.
Pair this with 52% of sampled households satisfied and 72% of the dissatisfied blaming close circles.
The reading: participation was real and partly captured.
worked_example.answer: A 9.6-point gap, which supports reading Kerala's Grama Sabhas as real but partly captured.

mistakes: Assuming one rule for every state. Article 243A leaves the Gram Sabha's powers to state law.
Treating a budget meeting as participatory budgeting when no money follows the vote.
Using MGNREGA provisions as current law after 1 July 2026 without checking the transitional rules.
Forgetting that Niyamgiri turned on who counts as the community.

recall.q: Which Article reserves not less than one-third of seats for women?
recall.a: Article 243D.

recall.q: What does PESA s4(e)(i) give a Gram Sabha?
recall.a: The power to approve plans, programmes and projects before the panchayat implements them.

recall.q: How many Gram Sabhas met in Niyamgiri in 2013, and what did they decide?
recall.a: Twelve, and all rejected the mining project.

recall.q: What three conditions did Kerala attach to its devolved plan funds?
recall.a: At least 30% productive sectors, at most 30% infrastructure, at least 10% for women's programmes.

recall.q: What did the Pune review find hardest?
recall.a: Moving from submitting a form to debating priorities with neighbours.

sections.title: Social audits and scorecards
sections.big_idea: Social audits and scorecards **join records to testimony** in public, so that officials and providers must answer.
in_plain_words: A financial audit checks records for the government. A social audit adds testimony and asks whether the work exists. The MKSS jan sunwai in Rajasthan began this by reading muster rolls aloud, and the idea became law in MGNREGA and its successor. Independence decides everything: a unit outside the implementing department, its own budget and the right to see every record.

The community score card gets users and providers to score a service separately on indicators they generate, then meet. The interface meeting turns complaint into negotiation. Whichever tool you use, **the follow-up hearing** is the step that makes findings count, and the question to ask of any system is how many findings led to recovery or action.

left.title: Financial audit
items: Done by auditors, for the government
Asks if money followed the rules

right.title: Social audit
items: Held in public, officials must answer

key_terms.meaning: Public hearing where records are read and tested.
Official list of workers on a work.
Andhra Pradesh's independent social audit society.
Users and providers score a service, then meet.
Session where scores are compared and actions agreed.

worked_example.title: Find the largest scorecard gap
worked_example.setup: Illustrative scores, 1 to 5, from the Pipalgaon anganwadi card: mothers versus workers on five indicators.
steps: Opens on time: 4 − 2 = 2.
Ration received in full: 3 − 2 = 1.
Far-hamlet children attend: 2 − 1 = 1.
Growth monitoring explained: 4 − 3 = 1.
Equal treatment of castes: 5 − 2 = 3. This is the largest gap, so it is the finding.
worked_example.answer: Equal treatment of castes has the largest gap, 3 points.

mistakes: Letting the department that spent the money run its own audit. That is self-assessment.
Skipping the last step. Schedule the follow-up hearing before the first one closes.
Turning the interface meeting into blame of an underpaid, overloaded frontline worker.
Generalising from one Ugandan trial without reading it beside the Indian evidence in section 9.

recall.q: What does a social audit ask that a financial audit does not?
recall.a: Whether the work exists, whether those listed worked and were paid, and whether it was worth doing.

recall.q: What did the jan sunwai join together?
recall.a: Official documents and villagers' testimony.

recall.q: What does independence of a social audit require?
recall.a: A unit outside the department, its own budget, community resource persons, the right to see every record and a hearing chaired by someone officials do not control.

recall.q: How many phases does the CARE score card toolkit set out?
recall.a: Five.

recall.q: Which social audit step is most often skipped?
recall.a: Tracking action taken and reporting back, the follow-up hearing.

sections.title: Photovoice, video and stories
sections.big_idea: Images and stories carry what interviews miss, but **consent for capture is separate from consent to show**.
in_plain_words: Photovoice lets people photograph their own lives, discuss the images in a group and take them to decision-makers. Participatory video began on Fogo Island with films screened back to the community, and Digital Green used farmer-made video in an agricultural trial. Most Significant Change collects stories and has groups choose in public.

The analysis rule is the same across all of them: participants' interpretation is data and the researcher's is a second layer. Images raise their own problems. A face, a shrine, a geotag or a first name can identify someone, and photographs of identifiable people are personal data. **Seek separate consent** for capture, discussion, exhibition and online publication.

diagram.caption: Most Significant Change as a loop

key_terms.meaning: People photograph their own lives and discuss the images.
1967 film-and-screening model that began participatory video.
Farmer-made video for agricultural extension.
Stories selected in public, with reasons recorded.
Films matter for the conversations they start.

worked_example.title: What the Digital Green trial counted
worked_example.setup: The deck reports a 13-month trial with eight control and eight experimental villages and 1,470 households.
steps: Total villages: 8 + 8 = 16.
Average households per village: 1,470 ÷ 16 = 91.9.
The reported multiples are seven times the adoption and ten times the cost-effectiveness.
The slide advises treating these as a promising early result needing larger replication.
worked_example.answer: 16 villages with about 92 households each; read the multiples as early results.

mistakes: Treating a photograph with location metadata as safe to share. Strip it before images leave the group.
Assuming consent to be filmed covers screening at the district office.
Photographing children without a guardian's agreement.
Quoting the Digital Green multiples as settled after one small, early trial.

recall.q: What are the three goals of Photovoice?
recall.a: Record and reflect strengths and concerns, promote critical dialogue, and reach policymakers.

recall.q: What was the guiding principle of the Fogo Process?
recall.a: Process over product: the films mattered for the conversations they started.

recall.q: Why is the selection the analysis in MSC?
recall.a: Recording why a panel chose a story shows what the organisation values.

recall.q: Name two kinds of image that can identify a person or community.
recall.a: Any two of: a face, a house, a shrine, a caste marker, a geotag, a caption with a name.

recall.q: What is the rule across all four visual analysis rows?
recall.a: Participants' interpretation is data and the researcher's is a second layer; report both.

sections.title: Participatory MEL and the evidence
sections.big_idea: The evidence on participation is **mixed and depends on context**: clear providers and cheap actions helped, diffuse collective problems did not.
in_plain_words: Participatory M&E lets communities choose some indicators and collect some data, alongside the standard ones funders need. Community indicators are closer to what people value but harder to aggregate, so keep a small standard core. Then read the evidence: Uganda's community monitoring cut child mortality, while Uttar Pradesh information campaigns changed nothing, and Indonesia's audits beat grassroots monitoring.

Reserved seats in West Bengal and Rajasthan changed what councils built. Mansuri and Rao's review of the field found modest gains in health and education, limited effects on income poverty and little lasting cohesion from induced efforts. To evaluate participation, measure **process, voice and power, outcomes and durability**, since an outcome can improve by a route that bypassed participation.

left.title: Uganda: it worked
items: Joint action plan with the provider
Specific target and person to hold to account

key_terms.meaning: Communities help choose, collect, interpret and decide.
A measure a community chooses, often closer to its values.
Better-off people taking a process's benefits.
Seats set aside for women, as under the 73rd Amendment.
Comparison showing what would have happened without the programme.

worked_example.title: Count the Uttar Pradesh villages
worked_example.setup: The deck's trial had three interventions of 65 villages each and 85 comparison villages.
steps: Villages in the three interventions: 65 × 3 = 195.
Add the comparison villages: 195 + 85 = 280.
Check against the stated total of 280 villages in Jaunpur district.
Only the third intervention, volunteer-run reading camps, improved outcomes.
worked_example.answer: 280 villages, which matches the stated total; only reading camps worked.

mistakes: Reading Uganda and Uttar Pradesh as proof about participation in general. The explanations offered were never tested against each other.
Promising income gains from participation alone, which the big review found limited.
Evaluating only outcomes and ignoring whether marginal groups' proposals reached the plan.
Taking the Indonesian result to mean participation is useless. It is one tool among several.

recall.q: Why keep standard indicators beside community ones?
recall.a: Funders need comparable indicators across districts, while villages need ones that answer their own questions.

recall.q: What did Olken find about raising audit probability from 4% to 100%?
recall.a: Missing expenditures fell by 8 points.

recall.q: What did Chattopadhyay and Duflo's study of reserved seats find?
recall.a: Women heads invested more in public goods close to women's concerns, such as drinking water.

recall.q: Name two of Mansuri and Rao's implications for practice.
recall.a: Any two of: pair participation with resources, do not promise income gains, plan for what survives, design for elite capture, budget for learning-oriented M&E.

recall.q: What are the four levels for evaluating participation?
recall.a: Process, voice and power, outcomes and durability.

sections.title: Doing it well: documentation and practice
sections.big_idea: Participatory work is rigorous when a reader can see **who produced each piece of evidence**, under what conditions and how conclusions followed.
in_plain_words: Reviewers dismiss participatory evidence as anecdote when the documentation is thin. Fix that with a same-day session record, triangulation across tools, groups, sources and team members, member checking, and a positionality statement that says how the team's caste, gender, language and funder might shape answers.

The Pipalgaon example shows a six-week sequence in which every tool runs in each hamlet before the village-wide meeting and findings return to each group first. Use the decision table to match purpose to approach, and apply the checklist before, during and after. The final test is simple: **what decision did the exercise change?**

events.what: Calendars and wealth ranking by group
Matrix ranking of priorities by group
Return findings; then full Gram Sabha

key_terms.meaning: Same-day note of who convened, attended, drew and argued.
Returning findings to participants.
Comparing across tools, groups, sources and team members.
How the team's identity shapes access and answers.
What an exercise is if only the project decides results.

worked_example.title: Check a session record
worked_example.setup: The deck's illustrative record: 23 people at peak, 14 women and 9 men, in the Dalit hamlet social map session.
steps: Check the headcount: 14 + 9 = 23.
Women's share of those present: 14 ÷ 23 = 0.61.
A high share of women present says nothing about who drew. The record shows two young men drew for the first hour.
Record that the landowner's presence for twenty minutes made people speak less.
worked_example.answer: 23 present, about 61% women, but the record also shows who drew and who limited speech.

mistakes: Photographing charts and recording nothing about who made them.
Building a single 'community view' from one meeting.
Compressing the timetable so that hamlet sessions are the first thing dropped.
Leaving positionality out of the report. It is a methods issue.

recall.q: What makes participatory work credible to a reviewer?
recall.a: A session record, triangulation, reporting of disagreement, member checking and an account of the team's own position.

recall.q: Name the four types of triangulation.
recall.a: Across tools, groups, sources and team members.

recall.q: What should you write before fieldwork about your team?
recall.a: A positionality statement covering caste, gender, religion, language, institutional link and funder.

recall.q: When should you write the session record?
recall.a: The same day.

recall.q: What does the final checklist question ask?
recall.a: What decision the exercise changed, and whether you can show it.

sections.title: Power, ethics and consent
sections.big_idea: A meeting is a political space, so design for **capture, silence and harm** before you design the exercise.
in_plain_words: Cooke and Kothari's critique made reflexivity about power standard. Elite capture can be open or quiet, and who speaks at a village meeting is not random: dominant-caste men sit at the front and women are often spoken for. Attendance counts mislead, since a list says nothing about who spoke or reached the minutes.

Consent works in two layers. The panchayat or Gram Sabha may permit an exercise, and each person still decides whether to take part. Group settings cannot promise confidentiality. Photographs, rankings and scorecards are personal data under the DPDP Act, with a research exemption that fails when data decides things about specific people. **Protect the people who speak up**, because speaking can cost something after you leave.

key_terms.meaning: Better-off people appropriating a process or its resources.
Participation as ritual, with decisions already made.
Head or authority whose permission may be sought.
India's data protection law; duties from 13 May 2027.
Examining your own power and position in the work.

worked_example.title: What an attendance list can show
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: an attendance list shows 50 attendees, 40% of them women.
steps: Women present: 50 × 0.4 = 20.
The list shows presence only. It cannot show whether any of the 20 spoke.
Add a column recording who spoke, and check the minutes for what women said.
Apply the table of signs: a list longer than the room suggests signatures collected afterwards.
worked_example.answer: 20 women attended; only a record of who spoke tells you whether they were heard.

mistakes: Taking the panchayat's permission as every individual's consent.
Promising confidentiality in a public meeting or hearing.
Using a wealth ranking to decide a benefit and assuming the research exemption covers it.
Leaving after a public hearing without follow-up, and so leaving witnesses exposed.

recall.q: What did Cooke and Kothari's critique make standard?
recall.a: Reflexivity about power in good practice.

recall.q: What does the ICMR guidance say about community engagement and consent?
recall.a: Community engagement does not replace individual informed consent.

recall.q: Name two design responses to elite capture.
recall.a: Any two of: separate meetings for marginal groups, published lists and criteria, secret ballots, independent audit.

recall.q: When does the DPDP research exemption fail?
recall.a: When the data is used to take a decision specific to a data principal, such as who receives a benefit.

recall.q: What is a sign that findings never reach the village?
recall.a: Nobody can say who has a copy of the map.

notes.2: The agenda runs from why participation matters, through its history and typologies, to tools, law, audits, stories, evidence and ethics. Sections 4 and 5 hold the PRA tools, and sections 10 and 11 hold the discipline for using them well. **Read section 11 before you go to the field.**
notes.4: Skip memorising the definition and keep the question the slide ends on: **who decides at each stage?** Every method here can be run extractively. Before you call an exercise participatory, write down who set the questions, who analysed the results and who holds a copy.
notes.5: Each justification implies its own test. Argue on instrumental grounds and you must show better results; on rights grounds, that power moved; on epistemic grounds, that you learned what the survey missed. **Pick the one your design rests on** and measure that, since most projects claim all three.
notes.6: On, with and by describe how much control people hold. Use them to place your own study faithfully. The mixing example is the practical part: a **fixed survey for prevalence** and a participatory map for missing hamlets answer different questions, so they can share one design.
notes.7: In India you work inside a legal frame whether or not your project document mentions it. Learn the four instruments in the table and what each gives a Gram Sabha. Sections 6 and 7 take them one at a time. Check the date: **status is as of October 2026**.
notes.8: Organic participation grows from activists, as the MKSS public hearings did. Induced participation is engineered through projects and schemes. The report's findings are modest: some gains in health and education, a limited effect on income poverty and **little lasting cohesion** from induced efforts.
notes.9: Pipalgaon is invented, so never quote its figures. Treat it as a rehearsal ground for each tool. Watch the Dalit hamlet across the stream, because the slide warns that **participatory work goes wrong first for those who live furthest from the meeting**.
notes.11: Freire's banking image treats people as empty accounts to be filled. Problem-posing education investigates a real situation together, starting from words and situations in people's own lives. Swap 'teacher' for 'project officer' as the slide suggests and **you have described much top-down planning**.
notes.12: Conscientizacao is awareness followed by action. Freire required dialogue built on respect, which is the hardest part to practise. A block officer who speaks for forty minutes before taking questions runs **a lecture dressed as consultation**. Notice what methods dropped from Freire: the political aim.
notes.13: Fals-Borda moved from research about peasants to research with peasant organisations. Remember the PAR cycle: knowledge is power, ordinary people produce valid knowledge, and research and action form one loop that the community owns. **Return findings in usable forms**, such as plays or pamphlets in the local language.
notes.14: Place Rahman as the South Asian strand of PAR: a Bangladeshi economist who studied the Bhoomi Sena movement and co-edited Action and Knowledge with Fals-Borda. The title names the target, **the professional monopoly over what counts as knowledge**.
notes.15: Chambers argued that outsiders misread rural poverty because of how they visit: briefly, along tarred roads, in the cool season, meeting the sarpanch. Memorise the correction as three moves: spend time, go off the road, and **let people show and analyse** while you listen.
notes.16: RRA aims at quicker learning by outsiders; PRA aims at analysis and action by local people. The slide calls the contrast a teaching simplification, and that is the point to keep: many 'PRAs' are **RRAs with chart paper**. Check who analyses before you accept the label.
notes.17: These figures show how much PRA was tested in India: 35 trainers from 18 institutions met in Bangalore in 1991, and MYRADA had worked in 2,000 villages in South India. Note the contributors named in the issue: MYRADA, AKRSP, SPEECH, Krishi Gram Vikas Kendra and ActionAid.
notes.18: Follow the timeline from Freire in 1968 to Cooke and Kothari in 2001. The lesson sits in the first paragraph: methods built for slow, open-ended work were squeezed into a few days to fit project timelines. **Success created the backlash** that section 11 examines.
notes.20: Typologies give you a vocabulary for degrees of participation, so a report can say which kind happened. They describe who holds power and never tell you which level is right, since a check dam's technical design may properly rest with engineers. **Argue for the level separately.**
notes.21: Learn the ladder as three bands: nonparticipation (rungs 1 and 2), tokenism (3 to 5) and citizen power (6 to 8). Arnstein's central claim sits under the figure: participation without redistribution of power is an empty ritual. **Read the rungs from the bottom up.**
notes.22: Rungs 1 and 2 aim to 'educate' or 'cure'; rungs 3 to 5 let people be heard while the powerful decide; rungs 6 to 8 move decision rights or budgets. Arnstein wrote for US planners. A signed attendance sheet later presented as consent is the slide's example of **nonparticipation**.
notes.23: Pretty's seven types run from passive to self-mobilisation. Read the table as a question about control. Material incentives show a useful test: **people stop when the incentive stops**. Functional participation means groups form after the major decisions are made.
notes.24: Functional and interactive committees look alike from outside: both meet, keep minutes and manage funds. The difference lies in where the objectives came from and whether the group would act without the project. **Ask for minutes from meetings the project did not attend.**
notes.25: White asks who wants participation and why. Read across each row: the top-down interest, the bottom-up interest, then the function. Nominal pairs legitimation with inclusion, and only the fourth row names one interest for both sides. **Name each actor's interest** before you design anything.
notes.26: One committee can be nominal for the agency, instrumental for the engineer and representative for the women who use it. Before an exercise, write down who wants it and why, for each actor. If the only interest you can name for the community is 'they will be included', **you are designing nominal participation**.
notes.27: Use the comparison to choose a lens. Arnstein asks how much power citizens hold, Pretty asks whether people's learning and action change, and White asks who wants participation and why. In the Pipalgaon example the three labels **point to the same fix**: meet in the hamlet first.
notes.29: The tools are simple and the discipline lies in running them. Memorise the six principles as a checklist: visual, group-based, sequenced, triangulated, shared, self-critical. Group analysis allows correction and creates pressure to conform, so ask every evening **who was absent and what was not said**.
notes.30: Follow the six steps in order: agree the purpose, draw boundaries, add households, mark attributes, cross-check, copy. The payoff is a sampling frame that often lists households the official lists miss, such as new settlers. **Cross-check against the voter list** and leave the original behind.
notes.31: The map shows whoever drew it. In Pipalgaon the first map showed 610 households and the hamlet across the stream added 140 more. Run groups by hamlet and by gender, and **treat the gap between maps as a finding**. Keep both maps.
notes.32: A resource map answers who has access to what, in which season. Overlay it on the social map to see which households depend on which resources. The caution is political: a map of forest use may later be read as **evidence of encroachment**, so agree in advance who keeps it.
notes.33: Walk the zones in order, from upland to stream, and fill the grid as you go. The data here is illustrative, and each column tells a different story about who uses the place. **Let residents choose the route after the first transect**, and record disagreements between walkers.
notes.34: Draw mobility maps separately for women and men. In the Pipalgaon example, distance costs money for men and permission for many women. The maps show where a service should be delivered and expose **seasonal migration** that a single-round survey can miss.
notes.35: Timelines begin with what people know, which makes them a respectful way to open fieldwork. They show earlier schemes that failed, so many 'new' proposals turn out to have been tried before. Record the anchor event behind each date and **present the result as the village's account**.
notes.36: Use the table as a recording sheet. A photograph of a map means little if you did not note who drew it, how many took part and what was argued about. Note who held the marker, since **drawing is a form of control**. A careful reviewer will dismiss output without this record.
notes.38: Plot variables by month with seeds, one variable at a time. The calendar shows hungry months, cash shortages, sickness peaks and the times people cannot attend. Use it to plan **your own work**: a gram sabha called at harvest is attended by those who did not leave, who are rarely the poorest.
notes.39: Read the chart as a group would. Farm work peaks from June to October, migration fills November to May, and illness peaks in July and August. Then draw the design consequences: **a March health camp reaches those who stayed**, and July work competes with farm work.
notes.40: Run the clock separately for women and men and by season. In the example the woman could name no free time while the man has two to three hours. Use it two ways: schedule meetings in hours each group called free, and **count unpaid time as a cost** when you ask women to contribute it.
notes.41: Wealth ranking produces local criteria of poverty, such as a widow without adult sons or a household that sold its draught animals. Compare the local piles with the official below-poverty-line or ration-card lists. Households poor by local criteria and **absent from the official list** are a common, useful finding.
notes.42: Ranking neighbours in public can shame or anger them, and labels travel. Take the safeguards seriously: small separate panels, numbered cards, several panels averaged, and a plain statement of what the ranking will decide. Ranking can help households apply for entitlements and **cannot replace the legal criteria**.
notes.43: In a chapati diagram, circle size shows importance and distance from the centre shows access. Look for large but distant institutions, small but close ones, and overlaps where one family runs several. Cut circles beforehand so people can **rearrange and argue**. Draw separate diagrams by gender and hamlet.
notes.44: Check the arithmetic yourself: farm ponds score 12, the common tank 14, fodder plots 11 and the concrete lane 8. The tank wins for this group. Run the same matrix with other groups, because a change in order is **the disagreement the gram sabha needs to discuss**. Criteria matter more than scores.
notes.45: Use the table to match question to tool and read the caution beside each. Then sequence the tools so each output feeds the next: social map for the frame, wealth ranking to place households on it, matrix ranking to ask the poorest group which works it would choose. **Every tool carries its own caution.**
notes.47: The 73rd Amendment made the Gram Sabha constitutional, yet Article 243A leaves its powers to state law, so they vary widely. Remember the one-third reservation for women under 243D. Before any participatory planning, **read your state's Panchayat Raj Act**, especially quorum and minutes.
notes.48: PESA gives each Gram Sabha in Scheduled Areas specific powers. Learn the sections in the table by function: safeguard customs and resources, approve plans, identify beneficiaries, certify fund use, and be consulted before land acquisition. **The powers reach a Gram Sabha through state law and rules.**
notes.49: Niyamgiri shows a participatory forum with legal standing changing a national decision. Twelve Gram Sabhas, seven in Rayagada and five in Kalahandi, all rejected the mining project, and the ministry rejected Stage II clearance in January 2014. The practical question it raises is **who counts as the community**.
notes.50: Participatory budgeting works with a real budget line, published rules, meetings in every ward, a vote and public tracking. Without money that follows the vote, it is consultation under another name. Keep two Indian examples in mind: Kerala at state scale and Pune at ward scale. **Money must follow the vote.**
notes.51: Read the numbers as design rules: 35 to 40% of state plan funds devolved, and the 30, 30 and 10 conditions on productive sectors, infrastructure and women's programmes. The scale was new, since a whole state's plan opened to village assemblies at once. **Ward Grama Sabhas were the main channel.**
notes.52: Hold two readings together. Grama Sabhas played a significant role in beneficiary selection, and 52% of sampled households were satisfied. Yet 72% of the dissatisfied cited preference for members' circles and 29% of beneficiaries never attended. **Participation was real and partly captured.**
notes.53: Pune shows a modest, durable model: simple forms, a regular annual cycle and a substantial allocation. The review also lists weaknesses, among them outreach, transparency, slum localities and public deliberation. The hard step is moving from **submitting a form to debating priorities** with neighbours.
notes.54: The 2025 Act repeals MGNREGA from 1 July 2026 and keeps village assemblies in planning and audit. Note s20(3), which obliges the panchayat to hand the Gram Sabha every record. Watch the rules under s20(2), since **the participatory quality of the audit will depend on them**.
notes.56: A financial audit works from records, for the government. A social audit works from records and testimony, in public, and asks whether the work exists. A road can pass the first and fail the second when half the muster roll names **belong to people who never worked on it**.
notes.57: The jan sunwai joined documents to testimony: a muster roll listing a dead man, read aloud before his widow. The hearings revealed how much depended on access to records, and the Beawar protest of 1996 fed the campaign for right to information laws. **Documents gave villagers' claims weight.**
notes.58: Use the table as a status check, as of October 2026. MGNREGA's s17 and the 2011 Audit Rules are repealed from 1 July 2026, the 2025 Act's s20 and s24(e) are in force, and Meghalaya has its own Act. If you audit works begun under MGNREGA, **check the transitional provisions in s37**.
notes.59: Who runs the audit matters as much as the law. Andhra Pradesh's SSAAT set the model for independence, with its own budget, trained resource persons from the community and the right to see every record. Apply one test: **how many findings last year led to money recovered or action** against an official?
notes.60: Follow six steps: obtain records, train resource persons, verify door to door, hold the hearing, record findings, track action. Verification writes up discrepancies case by case, with names. The last step is the one most often skipped, so **schedule the follow-up hearing before the first one closes**.
notes.61: The score card has five phases, and the interface meeting is the heart, turning complaint into negotiation. Users and providers score separately on indicators they generate, then meet. Phases two and three can run at once. **Plan the interface meeting first**, because everything feeds it.
notes.62: This is one trial in one country: 50 clinics, 25 treatment and 25 control, with a 33% fall in under-five mortality and 20% higher outpatient use. Hold it beside the Indian results in section 9 before you generalise. **Absenteeism fell** and health workers appeared to exert more effort.
notes.63: The finding is the gap. Mothers scored equal treatment of castes 2 and workers scored it 5, a difference of 3, the largest of the five indicators. Providers often rate themselves well on exactly what users rate worst. The interface meeting must make that gap **discussable without attacking the worker**.
notes.65: Photovoice has three goals: record strengths and concerns, promote critical dialogue through group discussion, and reach policymakers. Its first root is Freire, which links it back to section 2. It suits conditions that are hard to describe in an interview, such as an **unsafe route to school**.
notes.66: Participants hold the control: they choose which photographs to discuss, write the captions and decide what is exhibited. The researcher codes afterwards and reports the differences. Train for third parties in the frame, and **strip location from image metadata** before images leave the group.
notes.67: Participatory video began on Fogo Island in 1967, with films screened back to islanders. The guiding principle was process over product: films matter for the conversations they start. Before anyone presses record, **agree in writing who owns the footage** and who may edit it.
notes.68: Digital Green's trial shows promising early numbers: 16 villages, 1,470 households, adoption of some practices seven times higher and extension ten times more effective per dollar. The slide itself warns the trial was small and early. Quote the multiples as **a promising result that needs larger replication**.
notes.69: Follow five steps: agree categories, collect stories, select the most significant at each level, record the reasons, feed back. The selection is the analysis, since the reasons for choosing a story show what the organisation values. MSC complements indicators and suits **large, open-ended programmes**.
notes.70: Consent to record and consent to show are separate, and the second needs asking for each audience. A face, a shrine, a geotag or a first name in a caption can each identify someone. Seek **separate consent** for capture, discussion, exhibition and online publication, and offer blurring.
notes.71: Match each source to its analysis in the table. The rule across all four rows: participants' interpretation is data, and the researcher's interpretation is a second layer. **Report both**, including where they differ. The last column tells you what each report should contain.
notes.73: Participatory M&E lets communities define some indicators, collect some data and decide what changes. Most real systems mix the two, because funders need comparable indicators across districts while villages need their own questions answered. The MEL Basics 101 deck covers the conventional side this one **adds to**.
notes.74: Read each row as a pair: the standard indicator and one a community might choose. Community indicators are more sensitive to change and closer to what people value, but harder to aggregate. Keep **a small core of standard indicators** and let each community add its own, with its reasons.
notes.75: The trial had 280 villages: three interventions of 65 villages each and 85 comparison villages. Information meetings and report cards changed no one's participation. Only the volunteer-run reading camps improved outcomes, because individuals could act **without waiting for collective action**.
notes.76: Olken compared audits with grassroots monitoring across more than 600 village road projects. Raising audit probability from 4% to 100% cut missing expenditures by 8 points, while grassroots monitoring had little average impact. Participation is **one accountability tool among several**.
notes.77: Read the contrast as a prompt for design questions and no verdict on participation. The slide offers three: is there a clear provider, can the community sanction or reward that provider, and is the action cheap enough to take? These explanations are interpretations, and **context decides**.
notes.78: Random reservation of seats let the study isolate the effect: women heads invested more in drinking water and roads in West Bengal and drinking water in Rajasthan. Remember the division of labour: reservation guarantees presence, and **participatory methods then work on whether those present are heard**.
notes.79: Take each finding with its implication: pair participation with the resources a service needs, never promise income gains from participation alone, and plan for what survives the project. The review also found most World Bank projects lacked context and learning-oriented M&E, so **budget for monitoring that can change the project**.
notes.80: Evaluate on four levels: process, voice and power, outcomes and durability. The closing paragraph adds a warning: an outcome can improve through a route that bypassed participation entirely. Check **who attended, who spoke and whose proposals reached the plan** before you claim participation worked.
notes.82: Reviewers call participatory evidence anecdote when the documentation is thin. Rigour means a reader can see who produced each piece of evidence and how you moved from outputs to conclusions. Use member checking, triangulation and reporting of disagreement. **Be wary of findings that match the project's hopes exactly.**
notes.83: Fill the template the same day, field by field. Each row answers a question a sceptical reader will ask: who convened, who attended, who drew, what was disputed. Note the team-reflection row, where a landowner's twenty-minute presence made people speak less. **Record your own influence.**
notes.84: Triangulate four ways: across tools, groups, sources and team members. Treat disagreement as information, such as women ranking water first while men rank the road first. In the example the wealth ranking found 38 poor households **missing from the ration list**.
notes.85: Participants respond to who is asking. A team arriving in a government jeep will hear a different account from one introduced by a women's federation. Write a positionality statement before fieldwork, note in each record how your presence mattered, and **report it in the methods section**.
notes.86: Study the six-week sequence. Every tool runs in each hamlet before the village-wide meeting, and findings return to each group before the Gram Sabha. The closing warning matters: **compress the timetable and the hamlet sessions go first**, removing the people you most needed to hear.
notes.87: Use this as a decision table: match purpose to approach, then read the watch-for column. The closing advice works as a test. Ask who will decide what happens to the results, and if the answer is only the project, **choose a lighter method and call it consultation** in the report.
notes.88: Run the checklist at three moments: before, during and after. The last question is the hard one: what decision did the exercise change? If you cannot answer after six months, it was **consultation at best**, and saying so gives useful evidence for the next design.
notes.89: The Lab turns the deck into practice. Follow the suggested exercise: plan the Pipalgaon social map session using its mapping steps, fill in the positionality template for your own team, then compare your plan with the session record template from section 10. **Practise before your first field session.**
notes.91: Cooke and Kothari charged participatory development with the unjust and illegitimate exercise of power. Take from it a habit: treat the meeting as a political space with its own hierarchies. Ask who set the agenda, whose knowledge counted and who could afford to disagree. **The critique made reflexivity standard.**
notes.92: Elite capture can be open, through control of meetings and lists, or quiet, through who is told about the meeting. Link it to evidence you have met: Kerala's 29% and 72% figures and Olken's result. Capture is a matter of degree, so ask whether elite involvement **excludes others**.
notes.93: Attendance is necessary for voice and insufficient alone. An attendance list showing 40% women says nothing about whether any spoke or reached the minutes. Use the fixes on the slide: separate pre-meetings, neutral venues, a quorum rule that requires women's presence, and **recording who spoke as well as who came**.
notes.94: Use the third column on monitoring visits, since the answers are quick to check and hard to fake. Each sign maps to an earlier idea: committees that meet only when staff visit are Pretty's functional type, and no budget behind the vote is consultation. **Ask what the last rejected proposal was.**
notes.95: Keep two layers in mind: the panchayat or Gram Sabha may permit the exercise, and each person still decides whether to take part, what to say and what may be recorded. The ICMR provisions say community engagement does not replace individual consent. **Gatekeeper permission may be written or recorded, and should be witnessed.**
notes.96: Never promise confidentiality in a public meeting. Whatever is said at a mapping session or hearing is heard by neighbours. Say so at the start, ask people to keep others' contributions to themselves while stating that this cannot be enforced, and **offer a private conversation afterwards**. For children, use guardian permission plus assent.
notes.97: Photographs, rankings and scorecards with comments are personal data under the DPDP Act. The research exemption from 13 May 2027 applies only when the data is not used for a decision about a specific person, so a **wealth ranking that decides benefits** falls outside it. Number households and delete what you do not need.
notes.98: Speaking up can cost people after the team leaves. Anticipate retaliation, lost work, conflict between hamlets and backlash against women. Use the safeguards: agree what is said publicly, let groups present collectively, keep local legal aid contacts and follow up. **A team that exposes people and leaves has taken their risk.**
notes.99: Use the list as a reading path. The slide's own advice is to start with the Lab's community mapping exercise, then read the Qualitative Methods deck's section on focus groups before your first field session. Pick the strand that matches your gap: **ethics, data, MEL or community practice**.
